title: How many colours can a butterfly see?
blurb: We have three kinds of colour-sensing cells in our eyes. Scientists found a butterfly with at least 15 kinds.

cover.alt: Graphs of the colour-sensing cells of a person, a bee and a bird, and photos of two yellow butterflies that look different in ultraviolet light.
cover.credit: Figure 2, Chen, Stewart and Arikawa, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

source.name: Frontiers for Young Minds
source.title: The More, the Better? A Butterfly with 15 Kinds of Light Sensors in Its Eye
source.authors: Pei-Ju Chen, Finlay J. Stewart and Kentaro Arikawa

original.title: Extreme spectral richness in the eye of the common bluebottle butterfly, Graphium sarpedon
original.authors: Chen, P.-J., Awata, H., Matsushita, A., Yang, E.-C., and Arikawa, K.

cards.b: Your eyes have three kinds of light-sensing cells. One kind answers best to red light, one to green and one to blue. Your brain compares how strongly each kind answers, and that gives you every colour you see. Honey bees have three kinds too. How many kinds does a butterfly have? And does having more kinds mean seeing more colours?

Pei-Ju Chen and Kentaro Arikawa work with a team that studies insect eyes and brains at Sokendai, a university for advanced studies in Japan. Pei-Ju comes from Taiwan, an island rich in butterflies. Kentaro is a professor. Their team studied a butterfly called the common bluebottle and published the study in 2016.

Scientists cannot ask a butterfly what colours they see, so they measure the eye instead. They place a very fine probe, called an electrode, into one light-sensing cell. That cell sends a tiny electric signal when light it likes arrives. The team shines one colour at a time on the eye, from ultraviolet to red. Ultraviolet is light just past violet that our eyes cannot see. The signal shows which colours the cell answers to.

img.alt: Graphs of light-sensing cells in four animals, with many overlapping curves for the common bluebottle butterfly.
img.credit: Figure 3, Chen, Stewart and Arikawa, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: The common bluebottle butterfly has at least 15 kinds of light-sensing cells. That is the most ever found in an insect. A related butterfly, the Japanese yellow swallowtail, has six kinds. In some butterflies, males and females even differ. In the small white butterfly, only the females have cells that sense violet light.

Nobody knows yet if the bluebottle sees more colours than we do. Mantis shrimp have up to 16 kinds of sensors, but see colour poorly. The team thinks the bluebottle uses only four kinds for colour, like a close relative. The other 11 might spot fast movement against the sky, or mates and enemies. Only tests of butterfly behaviour can tell.

Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns that we cannot see but bees can. Male and female yellow butterflies look the same to us, but show different ultraviolet patterns. Learning how insect eyes work could help build drones that steer themselves like insects. It might also help farmers keep pests away with light instead of chemicals.

Light that looks white is really a mix of all colours. Split it. In a dark room, shine a torch onto the shiny side of an old CD, and let the bounced light fall on a white wall. A small rainbow appears. Name its colours from red to violet. This shows that white light holds many colours, and each kind of cell in an eye answers to a different part of it. Just past the violet edge is ultraviolet, which bees and butterflies can see.

img.alt: Coloured waves from red to violet, getting shorter, and a photo of a torch and a CD making a rainbow on a wall.
img.credit: Figure 1, Chen, Stewart and Arikawa, Frontiers for Young Minds, CC BY 4.0

cards.b: A butterfly with 15 kinds of light sensors may live in the same garden as you. But the garden probably looks very different to the butterfly. If every animal sees a different world, which one is the real garden? Is there one real colour, or does colour depend on who is looking?
